source_read: PMC full text PMC11916924 (author manuscript NIHMS2046083 of Ann Epidemiol 2024;102:8–22) in my own browser tab (title checked): abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results 1 to 2.3.2, Tables 1–3 (rendered as text), Discussion, Conclusion, acknowledgments, funding statement, declaration of interests, affiliations (read with javascript on my tab) and the reference list (entries 2, 3, 5, 17, 21, 31–48, 60, 61 checked). Figure 1 (PRISMA diagram): figure image not viewable (the image had not loaded and the screenshot of my tab came back blank), so exclusion reasons were not read. Card check only (task has no claims; step 1 empty).

design.note: A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with a stated three-database search, explicit criteria and duplicate independent screening, but no appraisal and no pooling. Filing it as narrative-review with the editors' checklist is workable; AMSTAR 2 would give critically low confidence anyway (no risk-of-bias assessment, no protocol), so the choice does not change what it can support.

key_findings.note: Methods › 1 and › 2 (single paragraphs) and Results › 1: 117 after duplicates, 76 and 24 excluded, 17 included (117 − 76 − 24 = 17); reference lists added none; no risk-of-bias assessment. Figure 1 not viewable in my tab either.
Results › 2, single paragraph (25%, 15–20%, 8%); Table 1 rows Denham (19.3%, 8%), Ruhm 2017 (25.4%, 19.5%), Tote (24.4% to 14.6%, 20.3% overall).

2.1.1 and Table 1 Denham row: OR 1.77 (1.08–2.90), 3.87 (2.32–6.46); 72% against 43%; lower odds with pathologist certifiers, investigation of violent deaths, required coroner training, centralized systems.

Table 2 Ruhm 2018 row (21–35%, 20–35%; 12.5 and 7.4 against 10.3 and 6.2; 23.1%, 26% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015) and Ruhm 2017 row (24%, 22% in 2014). The 2.2.1 text cites refs 33, 36 and 37 for the 21–35% and 20–35% range, but the table prints it only for Ruhm 2018.

2.2.1 (about 72% of unspecified unintentional deaths, 1999–2015) and Table 2 Buchanich row (about 70,000 reclassified; 'over 50% in 5 states'; rankings changed except 8 states). The table's 'over 50% in 5 states' does not say whether counts or rates rose; the card's 'count rose' is an interpretation. Checked against the primary paper (my buchanich_2018 reading), the card's note is right. Buchanich prints 'more than 70 000' of 97,159 unspecified deaths and never prints 72%. The over-50% increases are 2015 rates (Table 2: Alabama 94%, Indiana 85%, Mississippi 55%, Louisiana 99%, Pennsylvania 103%); for the same five states, counts 'more than doubled' over 1999–2015.

2.2.2 single paragraph and Table 2 (Quast: 8,633, 34%, 2003–2017; Horon: 1,052, 26%, 2012–2015; Lowder: 86.8%, 34.2% to 86.0%, 642). Checked against the primary paper (my horon_2018 reading), the card's note is right. Horon calls the 3,957 'total overdose deaths' without defining them, never 'all drug-related overdose deaths'. It does not print 26%: 1,052/3,957 = 26.6%, so Gutkind's 26% is truncated, not rounded. Two of Horon's four criteria count heroin markers present in toxicology.
2.2.2 and Table 2 rows for refs 44 (a quarter unspecified, toxicology for 89%, 44 deaths = 2%) and 45 (88%, 4.7%, 2.3%, 6%; 58% and 42%).

2.3.2 and Table 3 (Mertz: 66% of 112, i.e. 74 deaths, 171 to 245, 132 to 41, 34 to 5; Gill: 84/118 = 71%; Hurstak: 152 plus 20). The New York City '17%' increase cannot be checked from the review, whose table gives no base count of heroin deaths.

Table 3 Mallama row: DIM to NPDS 61:1 (the table says 'drug-related overdose deaths'; the study concerns opioid-involved fatal cases), multi-substance 77% against 58.6%, suicide 54% (commonly dispensed opioids) against 10%.
Discussion, 5th paragraph (refs 60 and 61). The review calls SAMHSA the 'Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Association'.

Discussion, 2nd paragraph (SUDORS 12 states in 2016, 47 states and Washington DC by 2019; heroin possibly underestimated in 2018–2019, ref 38), 3rd paragraph (coroner training and qualifications), Conclusion.

reporting_issues.note: National list printed as 17, 32–37, 40, 41; state list as 31, 40–46. Refs 38 and 39 appear in neither.
Ref 47 is Robinson (2017), a piece on county coroners; cited at '31,40–47', '31,44–47' and '40,41,44–47'.
Table 2: Ruhm 2016 and Ruhm 2018 probit models; Ruhm 2017 multiple imputation. The Discussion's 1st paragraph repeats 'multiple imputation methods' for all three.
Results › 1 calls it a manual search of the references; Discussion, 6th paragraph calls it a forward search.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high (appraisal and balance domains high). Reliance on own studies 'low' checked: no review author is among the named authors of refs 17 and 31–46 (refs 31 and 45 end in et al.).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, at its upper edge: the abstract says 'Across studies', but the 20–35% range is printed for one study (Ruhm 2018). Recomputed the card's editors' calculation: 1 − 1/1.20 = 16.7% and 1 − 1/1.35 = 25.9%, so about 17–26% (17.4% from the 21% lower bound for any opioid).

missed: Lowder (Table 2): the review says adding toxicology 'doubled' the opioid-involved share from 34.2% to 86.0%; that is a 2.5-fold rise (86.0/34.2 = 2.51), and the 642 added cases were recoded because an opioid was found in toxicology, which shows presence, not cause.

Results › 2 says the state and county studies covered seven states across the Northeast, South and West, but one of the seven is Indiana (Marion County), in the Midwest. The seven are California, Maryland, Florida, New York, Pennsylvania, Kentucky and Indiana.

Discussion, 1st paragraph calls the national 20–35% 'consistent with studies at the state level' (refs 40, 41). These are different measures. Horon's 26% is additional heroin-related deaths as a share of all overdose deaths. Quast's 34% is additional opioid-related deaths as a share of the NVSS count. Neither is a corrected opioid count comparable with Ruhm's.
Minor citation and spelling errors: Hurstak is dated 2017 in Table 3 and 2018 in the reference list (ref 31); 'Statitistics' (ref 3); SAMHSA misnamed (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

Figure 1 (PRISMA): image not viewable in my tab either; the 66% of imported records removed as duplicates (Discussion, 6th paragraph) implies about 344 records imported (117/0.34), which only the figure could confirm.
